title: Waymo Wins California Approval for Robotaxi Expansion Across 18 Counties
excerpt: The California Public Utilities Commission has cleared Waymo to operate its driverless ride-hailing service in Sacramento, San Diego, and expanded areas of the Bay Area and Los Angeles.
body:
• The California Public Utilities Commission on Friday approved Waymo to expand its autonomous ride-hailing service across 18 counties, covering nearly 250 cities — the largest geographic expansion of autonomous vehicle operations in state history.
  • The approval adds Sacramento and San Diego as new markets and significantly expands Waymo's operating area in the Bay Area and Los Angeles, including Napa/Wine Country and the East Bay.
  • Waymo previously received DMV approval for the same regions in late 2025. The CPUC clearance is the second regulatory step needed to charge passengers for driverless rides.
  • The company now operates more than 1,500 vehicles nationwide and completes over 250,000 rides per week across San Francisco, Los Angeles, Phoenix, and Austin.

The California Public Utilities Commission has given Waymo the green light to expand its autonomous ride-hailing service across the state, clearing the Alphabet-owned company to operate in 18 counties spanning nearly 250 cities. The decision, announced Friday, represents the largest geographic expansion of autonomous vehicle operations California has ever approved.

Where Waymo Can Now Operate

Waymo's approved territory now covers Alameda, Contra Costa, Los Angeles, Marin, Napa, Orange, Riverside, Sacramento, San Bernardino, San Diego, San Francisco, San Mateo, Santa Clara, Solano, Sonoma, Ventura, and Yolo counties. The expansion transforms Waymo's California footprint from three cities — San Francisco, San Jose, and Los Angeles — into a statewide network stretching from Wine Country to the Mexican border.

https://x.com/ElectrekCo/status/2088351774558097504

In the Bay Area, the approved areas now include most of the East Bay and North Bay, including Napa and Sonoma counties. In Southern California, the territory extends from Santa Clarita north of Los Angeles to San Diego. Sacramento, the state capital, is a new market entirely.

"We look forward to bringing the same mobility and safety benefits millions of Californians already enjoy to more communities, keeping local officials and residents informed every step of the way."

— Waymo, in a statement on X

A Two-Step Regulatory Process

The CPUC approval follows DMV authorization granted in late 2025 for the same regions. California requires both agencies to sign off before a company can charge passengers for driverless rides. With both clearances now in hand, Waymo can begin deploying its vehicles into communities across the expanded territory.

The company has emphasized that its expansion will be "gradual and guided by our safety framework." No specific launch dates have been announced for individual cities, though Waymo had previously targeted mid-2026 for San Diego and has been steadily building out operations nationwide.

Beyond California, Waymo operates in Phoenix, Austin, and Atlanta, and has announced plans to launch in Miami, Dallas, Houston, San Antonio, Orlando, Nashville, Minneapolis, New Orleans, Tampa, and London. The company currently runs more than 1,500 vehicles on the road and completes over 250,000 rides per week.

Implications for Bay Area Commuters

The expansion has immediate relevance for the Bay Area's Indian-American community, one of the largest in the nation. Waymo's extended coverage now connects Silicon Valley's tech corridors — where a significant share of South Asian professionals work — with broader East Bay communities, North Bay destinations, and Sacramento.

The potential for Wine Country trips without a designated driver has already generated buzz on community forums. More practically, the expansion could ease commute options for workers traveling between cities across the Bay Area's fragmented transit landscape.

Competition and Scale

Waymo's California expansion comes as the autonomous vehicle industry enters a pivotal phase. Tesla has launched a paid robotaxi service in Austin and has said it plans to expand to California later this year. Waymo, however, remains the only U.S. company operating fully driverless commercial services carrying paying passengers at scale.

The company is reportedly in talks to raise $15 billion in funding in 2026, capital that would support its rapid geographic expansion. The CPUC's decision suggests California regulators are increasingly comfortable with autonomous vehicles operating beyond tightly controlled urban zones — a shift that could accelerate adoption across the state.

What's Next

Waymo will roll out service in the newly approved areas on a city-by-city basis, though the timeline remains unspecified. The company has also been expanding its highway capabilities, recently beginning to offer rides that use freeways in Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Phoenix — a step toward longer-distance autonomous trips that could eventually connect the Bay Area to Sacramento or Los Angeles to San Diego.
